profile.address: 7505 John W Carpenter Fwy, Dallas, TX
profile.reading:
CoreSpace operates a data center at 7505 John W Carpenter Freeway in Dallas, Texas, a stretch of the corridor near Dallas Fort Worth International Airport that has long concentrated colocation and network facilities for North Texas. According to the company's own site, the Dallas facility totals 30,000 square feet of data center space. CoreSpace states company wide that its facilities are designed to deliver 99.995 percent uptime, with direct interconnection to major carrier networks and cloud providers, and that it has held Green Power Partner status for more than seven years, indicating a stated commitment to sourcing renewable energy for at least part of its operations. The company also states that its data centers, including this one, undergo third party audits for SSAE 18, HIPAA and PCI compliance, security standards commonly required by healthcare, financial services, and payment processing tenants who need documented controls before they will colocate equipment or run managed workloads in a third party facility.

CoreSpace itself describes its business as an infrastructure as a service provider founded in 2009, built around OpenStack for cloud scaling, Kubernetes for containerized workloads, and CEPH for consolidated storage, offered alongside traditional colocation, managed backup, DDoS protection, and disaster recovery services. The company operates a network of data centers across the United States and Europe, of which Dallas is one node, though its public materials do not break out a company history, prior ownership of the John W Carpenter Freeway building, or a customer list for this specific location.

What the company has not published for this facility is also informative. There is no disclosed power capacity in megawatts, no stated cooling architecture, no Tier certification from the Uptime Institute, and no confirmed account of the building's prior use or construction date, information some competing colocation providers publish as a matter of course to reassure enterprise customers evaluating physical infrastructure. The John W Carpenter Freeway corridor in Dallas has hosted data center and telecom facilities for multiple operators over the past two decades as the city grew into one of the largest interconnection markets in the country, and CoreSpace's presence there places it among a cluster of colocation providers competing for regional enterprise and cloud connectivity customers rather than hyperscale tenants, based on the scale of 30,000 square feet and the service mix the company advertises.

reading.body:
CoreSpace is a single-building colocation operator in Dallas with 30,000 square feet, 1 megawatt of conditioned power capacity, and under 30 percent utilization as of its 2025 sale listing.

The company exemplifies the long tail of US data center supply. Founded in 2009 by Liana Dunlap, CoreSpace serves roughly 200 mostly small and midsize business customers from one facility on the Dallas colocation corridor near DFW Airport, generating approximately 1.3 million dollars in 2024 revenue with six full time employees. Its business model combines traditional colocation with managed infrastructure services built on OpenStack, Kubernetes, and CEPH, the technology stack of small-to-midsize cloud operators rather than hyperscale consumers. The company states 99.995 percent uptime design, more than seven years of Green Power Partner status, and third party compliance certifications for SSAE 18, HIPAA and PCI, the controls required by healthcare, financial, and payment processing tenants.

The power picture reveals operational constraint. One and a half megawatts of utility service feeds the building, with one megawatt delivered to customer equipment and an on site generator for backup. Under 30 percent utilization means roughly 300 kilowatts of the conditioned power was in use at the time of the sale listing. This usage level reflects the business model: regional enterprise and cloud connectivity customers who need reliable carrier access and compliance certification but do not require the scale or economics of hyperscale facilities. CoreSpace publishes no Uptime Institute tier certification, no cooling architecture, and no building history.

The company's ownership status remains unconfirmed. In June 2025 the asset disposition firm Hilco Streambank announced CoreSpace for sale, covering real estate, hardware, IP addresses, trademarks and domain names, driven by founder retirement and leadership decision to exit. Non binding indications of interest were due June 17, 2025. CoreSpace's public website still advertises its services and names no new owner or change of control as of the research date. Whether the transaction closed is not established. If a sale completed, this operator record should become a former operator entry.
